The first 11 moves were identical to the second game, where Lee also played white. In the early game, Lee concentrated on taking territory in the edges and corners of the board, allowing AlphaGo to gain influence in the top and centre. Lee then invaded AlphaGo's region of influence at the top with moves 40 to 48, following the *amashi* strategy. AlphaGo responded with a shoulder hit at move 47, sacrificing four stones elsewhere and gaining the initiative with moves 47 to 53 and 69. Lee tested AlphaGo with moves 72 to 76 without provoking an error, and by this point in the game, commentators had begun to feel Lee's play was a lost cause. Franklin first convened a board of trustees for an organizational meeting on November 13, 1749. They opened a secondary school, the Academy of Philadelphia, in 1751. A collegiate charter was obtained for the [College of Philadelphia](/wiki/College_of_Philadelphia "College of Philadelphia") in 1755 and post-secondary instruction began shortly thereafter. It was the College of Philadelphia which ultimately was renamed the University of Pennsylvania in 1791. Penn considered 1749 to be its founding date until 1899, when the board of trustees voted to retroactively revise its founding date to 1740 in order to make the university older than Princeton University, which had been chartered in 1746. The 1740 date was selected because, in that year, a group of Philadelphians joined together to build a large preaching hall for the use of traveling evangelist [George Whitefield](/wiki/George_Whitefield "George Whitefield") who toured the American colonies delivering well attended open air sermons. The grand building was erected but, due to a shortage of funding, the interior was not furnished and the hall sat unused until Franklin's group purchased it in 1750. One best-of-5 play-in match was held before the Swiss stage between two teams.[[87]](#cite_note-90)

After a year as a gossip columnist for the *[Daily Express](/wiki/Daily_Express "Daily Express")*, Cartland published her first novel, *Jigsaw* (1923), a risqué society thriller that became a bestseller. She also began writing and producing somewhat racy plays, one of which, *Blood Money* (1926), was banned by the [Lord Chamberlain's Office](/wiki/Lord_Chamberlain%27s_Office "Lord Chamberlain's Office"). In the 1920s and 1930s, Cartland was a prominent young hostess in London society, noted for her beauty, energetic charm and daring parties. Her fashion sense also had a part, and she was one of the first clients of designer [Norman Hartnell](/wiki/Norman_Hartnell "Norman Hartnell"); she remained a client until he died in 1979. He made her presentation and wedding dresses; the latter was made to her own design against Hartnell's wishes, and she admitted it was a failure.

In 1950, Cartland was accused of plagiarism by author [Georgette Heyer](/wiki/Georgette_Heyer "Georgette Heyer"), after a reader drew attention to the apparent borrowing of Heyer's character names, character traits, dialogue and plot points in Cartland's early historical romances. In particular, *A Hazard of Hearts* (1949) replicated characters (including names) from Heyer's *[Friday's Child](/wiki/Friday%27s_Child_(novel) "Friday's Child (novel)")* (1944) and *The Knave of Hearts* (1950): Heyer alleged that "the conception ... , the principal characters, and many of the incidents, derive directly from an early book of my own, entitled *[These Old Shades](/wiki/These_Old_Shades "These Old Shades")*, first published in 1926. ... For minor situations and other characters she has drawn upon four of my other novels." Heyer completed a detailed analysis of the alleged plagiarisms for her solicitors, but the case never came to court.[[15]](#cite_note-Kloester275-15)

As well as writing novels, Cartland wrote a guide to married life in the 1950s, which was banned in Ireland.[[16]](#cite_note-16)

The **colonial colleges** are nine institutions of [higher education](/wiki/Higher_education "Higher education") founded in the [Thirteen Colonies](/wiki/Thirteen_Colonies "Thirteen Colonies"), predating the [United States](/wiki/United_States "United States"). As the only American universities old enough to have alumni that participated in the [American Revolution](/wiki/American_Revolution "American Revolution") and the [founding of the United States](/wiki/Founding_Fathers_of_the_United_States "Founding Fathers of the United States"), these schools have been identified as a group for their influence on U.S. history.[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2)

While all nine colonial colleges were founded as [private](/wiki/Private_university "Private university") institutions, two later became [public universities](/wiki/Public_university "Public university"): the [College of William & Mary](/wiki/College_of_William_%26_Mary "College of William & Mary") in 1906, and [Rutgers University](/wiki/Rutgers_University "Rutgers University") in 1945. The remaining seven are all members of the [Ivy League](/wiki/Ivy_League "Ivy League") and remain private to the present day: [Harvard](/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University"), [Yale](/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University"), [Princeton](/wiki/Princeton_University "Princeton University"), [Columbia](/wiki/Columbia_University "Columbia University"), [Penn](/wiki/University_of_Pennsylvania "University of Pennsylvania"), [Brown](/wiki/Brown_University "Brown University"), and [Dartmouth](/wiki/Dartmouth_College "Dartmouth College").

The group was formed through the purchase of 51% of [Kia](/wiki/Kia "Kia") by Hyundai Motor Company in 1998. As of 2011, Hyundai owns 33.7%[[4]](#cite_note-4) of Kia Motors.

In June 2021, [Hyundai Motor](/wiki/Hyundai_Motor_Company "Hyundai Motor Company"), [Hyundai Mobis](/wiki/Hyundai_Mobis "Hyundai Mobis"), [Hyundai Glovis](/wiki/Hyundai_Glovis "Hyundai Glovis"), and Hyundai Motor Group Executive Chair [Chung Eui-sun](/wiki/Chung_Eui-sun "Chung Eui-sun") collectively purchased an 80% stake in [Boston Dynamics](/wiki/Boston_Dynamics "Boston Dynamics"), which had been under [SoftBank Group](/wiki/SoftBank_Group "SoftBank Group")'s ownership.[[5]](#cite_note-5)

On May 22, 2022, the Hyundai Motor Group announced the company would invest an additional $5 billion in the United States by the year 2025. The investment would strengthen collaboration with US firms in areas such as [urban air mobility](/wiki/Urban_air_mobility "Urban air mobility"), [autonomous driving](/wiki/Autonomous_driving "Autonomous driving"), [artificial intelligence](/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence"), and [robotics](/wiki/Robotics "Robotics"). The investments were announced during a visit to South Korea by former President [Joe Biden](/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden").[[6]](#cite_note-6)

On December 10, 2024, Hyundai allowed customers to buy Hyundai cars on [Amazon](/wiki/Amazon_(company) "Amazon (company)"). They could pick it up at their local Hyundai dealership.
